claim: STM promoter activity is enhanced in the boundary domain of the shoot apical meristem.
source: We generated a transcriptional fusion pSTM::CFP-N7 with the 5,7 kb region upstream of the STM gene (AT1G62360) and observed the presence of an enhanced STM promoter activity in the SAM boundaries, as previously shown (Heisler et al., 2005; Leasure et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2003; Jurkuta et al., 2009), n > 20, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation of pSTM::CFP-N7 expression pattern in Figure 1A and cited literature.

claim: STM promoter activity is quantitatively correlated to Gaussian curvature in the boundary domain.
source: Using this pipeline, a negative correlation between CFP signal intensity and Gaussian curvature could be revealed and quantified (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figures 1C-E demonstrate statistical correlation between CFP signal and curvature.

claim: The correlation between STM promoter activity and tissue folding is maintained in the bot1-7 mutant background.
source: Whereas pBOUND>>GFP expression area was still correlated to tissue folding, we also observed a reduction in the area of GFP expression for a given primordium stage, when compared to the WT indicating a delay in pBOUND>>GFP appearance in bot1-7 (Figure 2D, WT: n = 154 measured on 5 meristems at 5 time points; bot1-7: n = 79 measured on 4 meristems at 5 time points).
evidence: Quantitative data from bot1-7 mutant analysis shown in Figure 2D demonstrates maintained correlation despite altered timing.

claim: The bot1-7 mutant exhibits a delay in tissue folding at the boundary compared to wild type.
source: As expected, we observed a reduction in folding angle for a given primordium size in bot1-7 when compared to the WT, demonstrating that the relation between tissue folding and organ emergence is impaired in bot1-7: large organs still have shallow boundaries (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: Comparative measurements between WT and bot1-7 shown in Figure 2A-C demonstrate reduced folding angle.

claim: The pSTM::STM-Venus translational fusion can fully complement the stm-dgh6 mutation.
source: After genotyping for the presence of the stm-dgh6 mutation, we could not distinguish the WT, stm-dgh6 heterozygotes and stm-dgh6 homozygote plants visually, confirming that pSTM::STM-Venus can fully complement the mutation (Figure 3D-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Phenotypic analysis of complementation shown in Figures 3D-F demonstrates rescue of mutant phenotype.

claim: STM expression at the boundary is required for organ separation.
source: Strikingly, major fusion defects were observed in most of the lines we generated, thus showing that organ separation was impaired in these lines (Figure 3K).
evidence: Observation of fusion defects in pSTM::STMamiRNA lines shown in Figure 3K demonstrates requirement for organ separation.

claim: The stm-dgh6 mutant exhibits two partly fused cotyledons and developmental arrest.
source: The stm-dgh6 mutant exhibits the typical stm phenotype with two partly fused cotyledons, at an angle divergent from 180°, and a development arrest. At the same stage, the WT can exhibit up to 8 leaves while the stm-dgh6  only displays two old cotyledons (Figure 3B).
evidence: Phenotypic description supported by observation in Figure 3B.

claim: DII-Venus signal is higher in the boundaries and correlates with pSTM::CFP-N7 expression.
source: Consistent with the characteristic localization of PIN1 transporters around the boundary (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Heisler et al., 2005), we also observed that a higher DII-Venus signal in the boundaries correlates with an increase in pSTM::CFP-N7 expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observation of co-localization shown in Figure 4A and cited literature support correlation.

claim: The correlation between DII-Venus and pSTM::CFP-N7 is stronger in the L1 layer than in the L2 layer.
source: Interestingly, while this correlation could also be observed on longitudinal sections through the boundary as it folds (Figure 4B), we also found that this correlation is stronger in the L1 layer: In the L2 layer, pSTM::CFP-N7 expression increased during crease formation, but this was not always correlated with an increase in DII-Venus signal (Figure 4B).
evidence: Layer-specific analysis shown in Figure 4B demonstrates differential correlation between layers.

claim: Application of synthetic auxin 2,4-D does not inhibit STM expression at the boundary.
source: In the same conditions, STM expression at the boundary was however either unchanged or even slightly increased (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental treatment with 2,4-D shown in Figure 4C demonstrates lack of inhibition.

claim: Application of 2,4-D dramatically decreases DII-Venus levels in the meristem.
source: As expected, DII-Venus levels were dramatically decreased in these conditions ([Brunoud et al., 2012]; Figure 4D), confirming that auxin could indeed diffuse into the meristem.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 4D and cited literature confirm auxin sensor response.

claim: STM expression and auxin depletion can be uncoupled at the boundary.
source: This suggests that, whereas auxin levels negatively correlate with STM expression in the meristem, this correlation is also dispensable: STM expression and auxin depletion can be uncoupled at the boundary.
evidence: Inference drawn from 2,4-D treatment experiments showing STM expression persists despite auxin presence.

claim: Global compression of the SAM leads to an increase in pSTM::CFP-N7 signal around 8 hours after compression.
source: Around 8 h after compression, we detected an increase of pSTM::CFP-N7 signal (n = 8; Figure 5B and Video 1).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging after mechanical compression shown in Figure 5B demonstrates temporal induction.

claim: Global compression of the SAM leads to an increase in pBOUND>>GFP signal.
source: Similar induction was observed in the pBOUND>>GFP line; although the GFP signal was more variable before compression, a strong induction could nevertheless be observed in the pBOUND>>GFP line after compression (n = 11; Figure 5C and Video 2).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging after mechanical compression shown in Figure 5C demonstrates induction.

claim: Ablation of a few cells in the meristem leads to a local increase of pSTM::CFP-N7 signal intensity around the ablation site from 18 hours onwards.
source: Strikingly, we observed a local increase of pSTM::CFP-N7 signal intensity around the ablation site from t = 18 h onwards (n = 16; Figures 5E and Video 3).
evidence: Time-lapse imaging after ablation shown in Figure 5E demonstrates localized temporal induction.

claim: The induction of STM after ablation appears stronger in larger ablations than in smaller ablations.
source: The induction also seemed stronger in larger ablations than in smaller ablations, consistent with a greater range of stress perturbation in larger ablations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of different ablation sizes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 demonstrates dose-dependent response.

claim: pBOUND>>GFP expression is induced after ablation with a delay compared to pSTM::CFP-N7.
source: A similar response was also observed in the pBOUND>>GFP background, again with a delay (n = 12; Figure 5F and Video 4).
evidence: Time-lapse comparison shown in Figure 5F demonstrates delayed but consistent induction.

claim: STM is never induced at the base of meristem after ablation, in the differentiating cells from the upper part of the stem.
source: We also noticed that with both markers, the induction of STM was not homogeneous around the ablation site. In particular, STM was never induced at the base of meristem, that is in the differentiating cells from the upper part of the stem.
evidence: Observation from ablation experiments indicates spatial restriction of induction response.

claim: The competence to express STM is limited to meristematic cells sensu stricto and cannot be overridden by mechanical perturbations.
source: This is consistent with the prevailing view from the literature stating that the competence to express STM is limited to meristematic cells sensu stricto, and our data suggest that such a prepattern cannot be overridden by mechanical perturbations.
evidence: Inference from spatial restriction of STM induction combined with established knowledge from literature.

claim: Whole mount in situ hybridization detected an asymmetric STM mRNA signal with higher intensity near the ablation site.
source: Even though this method is only semi-quantitative, we could detect an asymmetric signal, with a higher intensity near the ablation site, consistent with the results obtained with the pSTM::CFP-N7 and pBOUND>>GFP lines after ablation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, n = 9).
evidence: In situ hybridization results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 confirm reporter line observations.

claim: Incubation with 100 μM jasmonate overnight does not induce significant pSTM::CFP-N7 signal in most plants.
source: In these conditions, we did not observe any significant induction of pSTM::CFP-N7 signal in most of the plants (N = 10/14, Figure 5J), and slight fluctuations in CFP signal in the remaining ones (N = 4/14, Figure 5K).
evidence: Jasmonate treatment experiment shown in Figures 5J-K demonstrates lack of consistent induction.

claim: Wound-induced jasmonate is not the most likely candidate as a secondary messenger between stress and STM induction.
source: Yet, as this contrasts with the systematic and steady induction of STM after ablation and with the robust induction of a pJAZ10::GUS reporter by jasmonate (Figure 5L-O), wound-induced jasmonate is not the most likely candidate as a secondary messenger between stress and STM induction.
evidence: Comparison between ablation response and jasmonate treatment shown in Figures 5L-O supports inference.

claim: Isoxaben treatment leads to a global increase in pSTM-CFP-N7 signal intensity.
source: In these conditions, we could detect a global increase in pSTM-CFP-N7 signal intensity, when compared to that of the control (measurement on 10 nucleus of the central zone in the control (n = 6 meristems) and isoxaben-treated (n = 7 meristems); Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Quantitative measurements after isoxaben treatment shown in Figures 5G-H demonstrate increased signal.

claim: Isoxaben treatment induces pBOUND>>GFP expression.
source: This response was also confirmed in the pBOUND>>GFP background (control: n = 10, isoxaben: n = 20; Figure 5I).
evidence: Isoxaben treatment experiment shown in Figure 5I confirms induction in alternative reporter line.

claim: Mechanical perturbations cannot override the prepattern in the SAM as pBOUND>>GFP was not induced in the entire meristem after isoxaben treatment.
source: Note that pBOUND>>GFP was not induced in the entire meristem after isoxaben treatment, further demonstrating that mechanical perturbations cannot override the prepattern in the SAM.
evidence: Observation from isoxaben experiments demonstrates spatial restriction of mechanical response.

claim: STM expression can be modulated by mechanical stress in the SAM.
source: Because these different experimental setups have little in common except mechanical stress perturbation, we thus propose that STM expression can indeed be modulated by mechanical stress in the SAM.
evidence: Inference drawn from multiple independent mechanical perturbation experiments (compression, ablation, isoxaben).

claim: PID promoter activity is enhanced in the boundary domain of the meristem.
source: In a pPID::PID-YFP line, we observed a more abundant signal at the boundary of the meristem, as in the pSTM::STM-Venus line (Figure 6A).
evidence: Observation of pPID::PID-YFP expression pattern shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PID expression is not affected by ablation in both pPID::CFP-N7 and pPID>>GFP lines.
source: However, after ablation, PID expression was not affected in both the pPID::CFP-N7 and pPID>>GFP lines, in contrast to our results in the pSTM::CFP-N7 and pBOUND>>GFP line (Figure 6E–G, pPID::CFP-N7: n = 13; pPID>>GFP: n = 7).
evidence: Ablation experiments on PID reporter lines shown in Figures 6E-G demonstrate lack of response.

claim: PID expression is not induced by isoxaben treatment.
source: No induction could also be detected after isoxaben treatment in the pPID>>GFP line (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; n = 11).
evidence: Isoxaben treatment experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 demonstrates lack of induction.

claim: PID expression at the boundary may not depend on a mechanical signal.
source: Therefore, in our hands PID expression appeared as a negative control for our mechanical perturbations: PID expression at the boundary may not depend on a mechanical signal.
evidence: Inference from lack of PID response to multiple mechanical perturbations.

claim: The induction of STM by mechanical stress retains some specificity.
source: Conversely, it suggests that the induction of STM by mechanical stress retains some specificity.
evidence: Inference from differential response between STM and PID to mechanical perturbations.

claim: No significant induction of pCUC1::CUC1-GFP could be observed after ablations.
source: After ablations, no significant induction could be observed in the pCUC1::CUC1-GFP line (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; n = 11).
evidence: Ablation experiments on CUC1 reporter line shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 demonstrate lack of induction.

claim: CUC1 expression at the boundary is not controlled by a mechanical signal.
source: Altogether, this strongly suggests that CUC1 expression at the boundary is also not controlled by a mechanical signal.
evidence: Inference from lack of CUC1 response to ablation and pattern independence from wound position.

claim: A strong and steady induction of pCUC3::CFP signal was observed after ablation in all analyzed meristems.
source: In the pCUC3::CFP line, we observed a strong and steady induction of CFP signal after ablation in all the analyzed meristems (n = 20).
evidence: Ablation experiments on CUC3 reporter line shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 demonstrate consistent induction.

claim: CUC3 induction after ablation appears earlier than STM induction, as early as 6 hours after ablation.
source: Interestingly, this induction seemed to appear earlier than in the pSTM::CFP-N7 line, as a strong induction could be detected as early as t = 6 hr after ablation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Temporal comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 demonstrates earlier response.

claim: Boundary expressed transcription factors are not systematically induced by wounding.
source: Nonetheless this demonstrates that boundary expressed transcription factors, even from the same family, are not systematically induced by wounding and, thus, that the mechanical induction of STM retains some specificity.
evidence: Inference from differential responses of CUC1, CUC3, PID, and STM to mechanical perturbations.

claim: The relatively long time responses (8 to 24 hr) for STM induction after mechanical perturbations strongly suggests that the induction is indirect.
source: While this is consistent with the relatively slow timing of organ emergence and boundary folding in Arabidopsis meristems (Kwiatkowska, 2004; Reddy et al., 2004; Grandjean et al., 2004), it strongly suggests that the induction of STM expression after mechanical perturbations is indirect and could involve secondary signals, such as hormones.
evidence: Inference from temporal kinetics of STM induction combined with cited literature on meristem dynamics.

claim: Mechanical stress can affect the distribution of auxin in the SAM.
source: First, we checked whether mechanical stress can affect the distribution of auxin in the SAM.
evidence: Experimental question addressed through DII-Venus sensor experiments after mechanical perturbations.

claim: An induction of DII-Venus signal around the site of ablation was consistently observed after ablation.
source: After ablation and despite some variability in the basal level of DII-Venus signal on meristems recovering from NPA treatment (Figure 7A), we indeed consistently observed an induction of DII-Venus signal around the site of ablation (n = 21; Figure 7B, Video 5).
evidence: Ablation experiments with DII-Venus sensor shown in Figure 7B demonstrate auxin depletion response.

claim: The first effect of mechanical stress on DII-Venus signal was detected around 4 to 8 hours after ablation.
source: Interestingly, the first effect of mechanical stress on DII-Venus signal was detected around 4 to 8 h after ablation, which is consistent with the timing of the response of PIN1 after ablation (ca. 4 hr [Heisler et al., 2010]) and the subsequent response of pSTM::CFP-N7 after mechanical perturbation (8 to 18 hr after compression or ablation respectively, this study).
evidence: Temporal analysis of DII-Venus response compared with cited literature on PIN1 response and current study's STM data.

claim: DII-Venus signal is induced after compression.
source: The DII-Venus signal was also induced after compression (Figure 7C) further matching the response observed in the pSTM::CFP-N7 line.
evidence: Compression experiments with DII-Venus sensor shown in Figure 7C demonstrate auxin depletion response.

claim: Auxin patterns and mechanical stress fields act synergistically to control STM expression at the boundary.
source: Altogether, this suggests that auxin patterns and mechanical stress fields act synergistically to control STM expression at the boundary.
evidence: Inference from coordinated temporal responses of DII-Venus and STM reporters to mechanical perturbations.

claim: No DII-Venus signal could be detected in pin1-6 pseudo-boundaries.
source: Despite the variability in DII-Venus signal in the pin1-6 meristems, we could not detect any DII-Venus signal in pin1-6 pseudo-boundaries, suggesting that PIN1 is necessary to deplete auxin from the boundary (Figure 7D, n = 6).
evidence: Analysis of DII-Venus in pin1-6 mutant shown in Figure 7D demonstrates requirement for PIN1.

claim: Both pBOUND>>GFP and pSTM::CFP-N7 signals are present in pin1-6 pseudo-boundaries.
source: Interestingly, both pBOUND>>GFP and pSTM::CFP-N7 signals were present in the pin1-6 pseudo-boundaries (Figure 7D and E), thus suggesting that PIN1 is not a major player in the correlation between tissue folding and STM expression.
evidence: Analysis of STM reporters in pin1-6 mutant shown in Figures 7D-E demonstrates PIN1-independent expression.

claim: No significant induction of DII-Venus signal could be detected after ablation in pin1-6.
source: No significant induction of DII-Venus signal could be detected after ablation in pin1-6 demonstrating that auxin depletion after ablation mainly relies on PIN1 (n = 11, Figure 7G; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Ablation experiments in pin1-6 mutant shown in Figure 7G demonstrate PIN1 requirement for auxin response.

claim: Both pSTM::CFP-N7 and pBOUND>>GFP are systematically induced around the site of ablation in pin1-6.
source: However, both pSTM::CFP-N7 and pBOUND>>GFP were systematically induced around the site of ablation (Figure 7F and G; Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and 2).
evidence: Ablation experiments in pin1-6 mutant shown in Figures 7F-G demonstrate STM induction despite PIN1 absence.

claim: The induction of STM after ablation can occur independently of PIN1.
source: This demonstrates that the induction of STM after ablation can occur independently of PIN1.
evidence: Inference from observation of STM induction in pin1-6 mutant after ablation.

claim: The induction of STM around the ablation site could not be clearly correlated with DII-Venus signal intensity in pin1-6.
source: While we cannot rule out the possibility that other auxin carriers substitute for PIN1 in the pin1 background, despite our efforts, the induction of STM around the ablation site could not be clearly correlated with DII-Venus signal intensity, suggesting that the induction of STM after an ablation is not primarily caused by a local reduction in auxin levels.
evidence: Analysis of spatial correlation between STM and DII-Venus in pin1-6 after ablation shows lack of correspondence.

claim: STM expression and auxin distribution can be partially uncoupled.
source: In other words, STM expression and auxin distribution can be partially uncoupled and the correlation between tissue folding and STM expression always remains.
evidence: Inference from pin1-6 experiments showing STM induction without corresponding auxin depletion.

claim: Oryzalin-triggered tissue folding leads to a slight increase of GFP and CFP signals in the young boundaries in both pBOUND>>GFP and pSTM::CFP-N7 lines.
source: In both the pBOUND>>GFP and pSTM::CFP-N7 lines, oryzalin-triggered tissue folding led to a slight increase of GFP and CFP signals respectively, in the young boundaries (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Oryzalin application experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3 demonstrate induction.

claim: Mechanical stress can promote the expression of STM at the boundary relatively independently of auxin distribution.
source: Because this induction occurred in the presence of NPA and as oryzalin indirectly modifies the mechanical status of cell walls (and thus promotes organ emergence), this further supports a scenario in which mechanical stress can promote the expression of STM at the boundary, relatively independently of auxin distribution.
evidence: Inference from oryzalin experiments in presence of NPA showing STM induction without auxin transport.

claim: The patterning genes Twist and Notail are induced by embryo deformation during gastrulation and epiboly in Drosophila and Zebrafish embryos through activation of the β-catenin pathway.
source: For instance, the patterning genes Twist and Notail are induced by the deformation of the embryo during gastrulation and epiboly in Drosophila and Zebrafish embryos respectively, through the activation of the β-catenin pathway (Brunet et al., 2013; Farge, 2003; Desprat et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for mechanically-induced gene expression in animal development.

claim: The expression of STM at the boundary of the shoot apical meristem is correlated with tissue folding.
source: Our observations are in line with these conclusions: we report that the expression of STM at the boundary of the shoot apical meristem is correlated with tissue folding and is increased by mechanical stress.
evidence: Summary statement supported by multiple experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: Biochemical factors such as auxin promote differential growth and shape changes in the meristem, which generate mechanical signals that can impact the expression of regulators.
source: This provides a scenario in which biochemical factors, such as auxin, promote differential growth and shape changes in the meristem, which in turn, generate mechanical signals that can impact the expression of some of these regulators.
evidence: Proposed model integrating experimental findings on auxin, mechanical stress, and STM expression.

claim: Mechanical stress at the boundary contributes to the local expression of STM that is necessary for the separation between organs.
source: Here we show that mechanical stress at the boundary contributes to the local expression of STM that is in turn necessary for the separation between organs.
evidence: Summary statement integrating mechanical perturbation experiments and STM knockdown phenotypes.

claim: Tensile stress at the meristem boundary becomes anisotropic before tissue folds, as maximal stress direction is first prescribed by differential growth.
source: Note that tensile stress at the meristem boundary becomes anisotropic before tissue folds, as maximal stress direction is first prescribed by differential growth.
evidence: Statement based on established understanding of mechanical stress patterns in growing tissues.

claim: Overexpression of class I KNOX genes is sufficient to induce ectopic meristems.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of class I KNOX genes is sufficient to induce ectopic meristems (Chuck et al., 1996).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for KNOX gene function in meristem formation.

claim: The boundary is where auxin is redistributed from the adjacent neighboring organ to the meristematic pool where new organs or new axis need to be initiated.
source: The boundary also plays a crucial role in plant architecture: this is where auxin is redistributed from the adjacent neighboring organ to the meristematic pool where new organs or new axis need to be initiated (Heisler et al., 2005; Reinhardt et al., 2003; de Reuille et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for auxin dynamics at the boundary.

claim: The response to mechanical stress can uncouple STM expression from auxin depletion.
source: While we provide further evidence supporting a strong coordination between STM expression and auxin depletion, we also found that the response to mechanical stress can uncouple them.
evidence: Summary statement integrating findings from auxin treatment and pin1 mutant experiments.

claim: Mechanical perturbations induce STM expression even when auxin transport or level is affected.
source: In particular, mechanical perturbations induce STM expression even when auxin transport or level is affected.
evidence: Summary of findings from 2,4-D treatment, pin1 mutant, and NPA+oryzalin experiments.

claim: Mechanical stress does not impact the expression of PINOID.
source: In addition, mechanical stress does not seem to impact the expression of PINOID, which has been associated with the control of PIN1 polarity and thus auxin patterns in the meristem (Robert and Offringa, 2008).
evidence: Summary of PID reporter experiments combined with cited literature on PID function.

claim: The absence of strict coupling between auxin depletion and mechanical stress adds robustness to meristem functions at the boundary.
source: We propose that the absence of a strict coupling between auxin depletion and mechanical stress is a way to add robustness in meristem functions at the boundary.
evidence: Proposed interpretation of the partial uncoupling between auxin and mechanical signaling.

claim: STM promotes the expression of the cytokinin biosynthesis gene AtIPT7 and cytokinin response factor ARR5.
source: Activation of STM promotes the expression of the cytokinin biosynthesis gene AtIPT7 and cytokinin response factor ARR5 (Yanai et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for STM-cytokinin interaction.

claim: Overproduction or application of cytokinins increase the expression level of STM and can rescue weak stm mutant alleles.
source: Conversely, overproduction or application of cytokinins increase the expression level of STM and can rescue weak stm mutant alleles (Rupp et al., 1999; Jasinski et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for cytokinin effects on STM expression.

claim: The level of cytokinins has been predicted to increase in the boundary based on the pTCS signal.
source: Interestingly, the level of cytokinins has been predicted to increase in the boundary, based on the cytokinin activity reporter pTCS signal, and axillary meristem formation has been shown to require cytokinin signalling (Wang et al., 2014), consistent with the well-known bushy phenotypes of cytokinin overproducers.
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for cytokinin distribution and function at the boundary.

claim: Class I KNOX proteins reduce gibberellins levels through direct repression of the GA-20 oxidase gene.
source: Class I KNOX proteins also reduce gibberellins levels, notably through a direct repression of the GA-20 oxidase gene (Sakamoto et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2004); conversely gibberellins can rescue the phenotype of KNOX overexpressors (Hay et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for KNOX-gibberellin interaction.

claim: The induction of the gibberellin catabolism gene GA-2 oxidase depends on KNOX proteins.
source: The induction of the gibberellin catabolism gene GA-2 oxidase was also shown to depend on KNOX proteins (Jasinski et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for KNOX regulation of gibberellin metabolism.

claim: Ethylene restricts the expression of class I KNOX gene KNAT2 in the shoot meristem to the boundary domain.
source: Interestingly, ethylene restricts the expression of class I KNOX gene KNAT2 in the shoot meristem to the boundary domain (Hamant et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for ethylene regulation of KNOX gene expression.

claim: Ethylene response mutants still display thigmomorphogenesis in response to touch despite touch inducing ethylene synthesis.
source: For instance, while touch can induce ethylene synthesis, ethylene response mutants still display thigmomorphogenesis in response to touch (Chehab et al., 2012); touch-induced thigmomorphogenesis rather depends on jasmonate (Chehab et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited literature provides evidence for hormone involvement in mechanoperception.

claim: The robustness of complex morphogenetic regulation may rely on a dialog between gene and form where shape constrains possible outputs of the gene regulatory network.
source: Here we have investigated whether the shape itself, and its associated mechanics, interferes with gene expression and channels morphogenesis by constraining the possible outputs of the gene regulatory network. If generalized, such a dialog between gene and form could help us understand how reproducible shapes can emerge from a complex gene regulatory network that is susceptible to noise.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on integration of study findings with broader developmental biology concepts.
